Motion perception deficit in schizophrenia is not solely caused by an eye-tracking abnormality. While speed discrimination, per se, is not impaired in schizophrenia patients, the observed abnormality appears to be a consequence of impairment in generating or integrating feedback information from eye movements. This study highlights the importance of concurrently measuring eye movements to understand interactions between these two systems.

In other words, while the eyes move normally and can track moving objects with ease, the brain may have difficulty processing this movement information correctly, leading to motion perception deficits. This deficit is not due to an issue with tracking or focusing on specific visual stimuli but rather a broader problem in integrating sensory information from both the eyes and brain.

It's also worth noting that while eye-tracking can be a useful tool for studying motion perception, it may not always capture the full complexity of this process. Other factors, such as cognitive processing and attention, play a role in determining how we perceive motion, and may not be fully captured by traditional eye-tracking measures.
